intro: You will rarely write an inference engine, but you will choose, deploy, tune and operate one. Three open-source engines dominate datacenter LLM serving: vLLM, SGLang and NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM. All three expose an OpenAI-compatible API and share the same core ideas, but they differ in where they shine. This lesson gets each one running locally, explains what each optimises, and gives you a way to choose that is grounded in your own benchmarks rather than someone else's chart.
objectives: Launch vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM as OpenAI-compatible servers
Explain the features all modern engines share and where they differ
Choose an engine based on hardware, workload shape and operational needs
Run the same client against any engine by changing only the base URL
Place lighter local runtimes such as llama.cpp correctly for development

blocks.text: The engines have converged on the same toolkit, so learn it once. **Continuous batching** adds and removes requests at every step. **Paged KV-cache management** allocates cache in blocks. **Prefix caching** reuses cache for shared prompt prefixes. **Chunked prefill** keeps long prompts from stalling decode. **CUDA graphs** and fused kernels cut launch overhead. **Quantization** (FP8 and 4-bit formats), **tensor and pipeline parallelism**, **speculative decoding**, **LoRA adapters**, **structured output** and tool-call parsing are standard features.

Because all three speak the OpenAI API, your application, gateway and benchmark client do not change when you switch engines; only the base URL and model name do. That makes trying several engines on your own workload cheap, and it is the right way to decide.

The differences that remain are in defaults, kernels and focus: which models and GPUs get optimised first, how aggressively each engine schedules prefill against decode, how its prefix cache is indexed, how it exposes metrics, and how often it releases. Those differences can swing results by large margins on one workload and vanish on another, which is why the comparison below ends with a benchmark rather than a verdict.

vLLM is the broad, community default: the widest model and hardware support (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, TPUs and more through plugins), PagedAttention, a large feature set and a big ecosystem that includes KServe runtimes, a production-stack Helm chart and integration in distributed frameworks such as Dynamo and llm-d. Pick it when you want the safest general choice. The open-source track's vLLM lesson covers its flags and metrics in depth.

blocks.caption: vLLM on port 8000
blocks.code:
export MODEL_ID=YOUR_ORG/YOUR_MODEL
uv pip install vllm
vllm serve "$MODEL_ID" --port 8000 --max-model-len 8192

blocks.text: SGLang is a high-performance engine whose signature is **RadixAttention**: the KV cache is kept in a radix tree keyed by token prefixes, so any request that shares a prefix with earlier work, a multi-turn conversation, an agent re-sending its scratchpad, few-shot templates, reuses it automatically. It is strong for agentic and multi-turn workloads, structured generation, and large mixture-of-experts models, and it is widely used for reinforcement-learning rollouts.

blocks.caption: SGLang (its docs use port 30000)
blocks.code:
uv pip install --prerelease=allow sglang
sglang serve "$MODEL_ID" --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

blocks.text: TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA's engine, with kernels tuned for each NVIDIA GPU generation, early support for new hardware features and low-precision formats, and in-flight batching. Older versions required compiling a per-model engine ahead of time; current releases default to a PyTorch-based backend that loads checkpoints directly. `trtllm-serve` gives an OpenAI-compatible server, `trtllm-bench` benchmarks, and it also runs behind Triton or Dynamo. Pick it when you are all-in on NVIDIA and want the most from the newest GPUs.

For laptops and CPUs, llama.cpp and tools built on it run quantized GGUF models without a datacenter GPU. They are excellent for development and edge devices, not a substitute for a batching datacenter engine under heavy concurrent load.

sections.heading: Choosing, and the same client for all

rows: Broadest model and hardware support, biggest ecosystem
Heavy prefix reuse: multi-turn chat, agents, structured generation
Maximum performance on the newest NVIDIA GPUs and formats

blocks.text: Treat the table as a starting hypothesis. Performance rankings change with every release, model and GPU. Run your real prompt and output length distribution through each candidate at your target latency, compare goodput per GPU, and weigh operational factors: container images, metrics, upgrade cadence, model support for what you will serve next year.

blocks.caption: One client, any engine: only the base URL changes
blocks.code:
from openai import OpenAI

for base in ["http://localhost:8000/v1", "http://localhost:30000/v1"]:
    client = OpenAI(base_url=base, api_key="not-needed-locally")
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=client.models.list().data[0].id,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "One sentence on KV caches."}],
        max_tokens=60,
    )
    print(base, reply.choices[0].message.content)

practice.title: Two engines, one workload
steps: On a single-GPU machine, start vLLM on port 8000 with a small open model and `--max-model-len 8192`.
Run the client above against it and confirm it answers.
Stop vLLM, start SGLang on port 30000 with the same model, and rerun the client unchanged except for the URL.
Write a 20-turn conversation script that re-sends the growing history each turn and record TTFT per turn on each engine.
Note memory used after startup on each engine with `nvidia-smi` and the KV-cache capacity each logs.
Write down which engine you would pick for this workload and why, citing your numbers.

focus: All three engines share continuous batching, paged cache, prefix caching, chunked prefill and quantization.
All speak the OpenAI API: switching engines means changing a URL.
vLLM: broadest support and ecosystem. SGLang: RadixAttention prefix reuse. TensorRT-LLM: NVIDIA-tuned.
Decide with your own workload, at your latency target, per GPU.
llama.cpp for laptops and edge, not for high-concurrency serving.
Weigh operations (images, metrics, upgrades), not just speed.

items.desc: Point any OpenAI client at the engine
Draft tokens cheaply, verify in one pass
Many fine-tunes on one base model
Engine-neutral benchmark against any OpenAI-compatible URL

pitfalls: Choosing an engine from a vendor chart measured on someone else's workload.
Comparing engines at different max context lengths or precisions.
Ignoring operational fit: images, metrics, upgrade cadence, model support.
Using a laptop runtime for a high-concurrency production endpoint.
Tying application code to one engine's non-standard API.

quiz.q: Your app moves from vLLM to SGLang. What must change in a client written with the OpenAI SDK?
options: Only the base URL and possibly the model name
The whole request format, because SGLang uses gRPC only
The tokenizer, which the client must now run itself
Nothing at all, even the URL stays the same
quiz.explain: Both engines expose OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so the client keeps its code and points at a different base URL, with the model name the new server reports.

quiz.q: An agent re-sends a growing 10,000-token scratchpad on every step. Which engine feature matters most?
options: Prefix reuse such as SGLang's RadixAttention
Ahead-of-time engine compilation
CPU offload of model weights
Higher sampling temperature
quiz.explain: The shared prefix can be served from cache instead of recomputed. RadixAttention indexes cache by token prefix to do this automatically; vLLM's prefix caching does the same job.

quiz.q: A team wants the best performance from the newest NVIDIA GPUs and new low-precision formats as soon as they ship. Which engine is the natural first candidate?
options: TensorRT-LLM
llama.cpp
A CPU-only runtime
None, because engines all perform identically
quiz.explain: TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA's engine, with kernels tuned per GPU generation and early support for new hardware features. Always confirm with your own benchmark.

quiz.q: Which statement about choosing an engine is most defensible?
options: Benchmark candidates on your own workload at your latency target
Pick whichever engine has the most GitHub stars
Always use the engine with the highest peak tokens per second chart
Use a different engine for every model to compare them in production
quiz.explain: Rankings depend on model, GPU, release and workload shape. Goodput per GPU on your real traffic, plus operational fit, is what matters.

quiz.q: Where does a llama.cpp-based runtime fit best?
options: Development on laptops, CPUs and edge devices
The main high-concurrency datacenter endpoint
Tensor-parallel serving across eight GPUs
Disaggregated prefill and decode clusters
quiz.explain: It runs quantized models efficiently on modest hardware, ideal locally and at the edge, but it is not built for the continuous-batching, multi-GPU scale of datacenter engines.
